## Chapter 1

One day in June, 1854, young Adams walked for the last time down the steps of Mr. Dixwell's school in Boylston Place, and felt no sensation but unqualified joy. He was born too old for school. The same could be said of most New England boys; mentally they never were boys, and these first six years of education were wasted in doing imperfectly what might have been done perfectly in one. The next regular step was Harvard College. For generation after generation, Adamses and Brookses and Boylstons and Gorhams had gone there, and although none, as far as known, had ever done any good there, custom kept each generation in the track. No one took Harvard College seriously. All went because their friends went, and the College was their ideal of social self-respect.

Harvard, as far as it educated at all, was a mild and liberal school, which sent young men into the world with all they needed to make respectable citizens. Leaders of men it never tried to make. The Unitarian clergy had given to the College a character of moderation, balance, judgment, restraint, what the French called *mesure*; excellent traits, which the College attained with singular success, so that its graduates could commonly be recognized by the stamp. In effect, the school created a type but not a will. Four years of Harvard College, if successful, resulted in an autobiographical blank, a mind on which only a water-mark had been stamped.

The stamp was a good one. The chief wonder of education is that it does not ruin everybody concerned in it, teachers and taught. Harvard College was probably less hurtful than any other university then in existence; it taught little, and that little ill, but it left the mind open, free from bias, ignorant of facts, but docile. The graduate had few strong prejudices. He knew little, but his mind remained supple, ready to receive knowledge.

What caused the boy most disappointment was the little he got from his mates. The Class of 1858 was a typical collection of young New Englanders: quietly penetrating and aggressively commonplace; free from meannesses, jealousies, intrigues, enthusiasms, and passions; not exceptionally quick; singularly indifferent to display; distrustful of themselves, but little disposed to trust any one else; not much humor of their own, but full of readiness to enjoy the humor of others; negative to a degree that in the long run became positive and triumphant. They never flattered, seldom praised; their judgment beyond appeal, not an act of intellect or emotion or will, but a sort of gravitation. This was Harvard College incarnate.

Into this dissolvent medium, chance tossed a trio of Virginians as little fitted for it as Sioux Indians to a treadmill. One was the son of Colonel Robert E. Lee. "Roony" Lee was a Virginian of the eighteenth century, much as Adams was a Bostonian of the same age—tall, handsome, genial, with the habit of command. For a year he was the most popular young man in his class, then slowly dropped into the background. Strictly, the Southerner had no mind; he had temperament. He could not analyze an idea, and could not even conceive of admitting two; but in life one could get along very well without ideas, if one had only the social instinct. The lesson was vital to these young men, who within ten years killed each other by scores in the act of testing their college conclusions. Adams liked the Virginians, and their friendship was unbroken even when prejudice ran hot; yet he had begun to fear that one eighteenth-century type might not differ deeply from another. He himself was little more fit than the Virginians to deal with a future America which showed no fancy for the past—a Northern society already preferring economists over diplomats or soldiers.

If the student got little from his mates, he got little more from his masters. The four years passed at college were, for his purposes, wasted. He stood graded precisely in the middle. In mathematics he never reached the alphabet of a language he most needed to read. Beyond two or three Greek plays, he got nothing from the ancient languages; beyond some incoherent theories of free trade, little from Political Economy. He never heard the name of Karl Marx mentioned, or the title of "Capital." He was equally ignorant of Auguste Comte. The only teaching that appealed to his imagination was a course of lectures by Louis Agassiz on the Glacial Period and Paleontology, which had more influence on his curiosity than the rest of the college instruction altogether. The entire work of the four years could have been put easily into the work of any four months of after life.

Harvard College was a negative force, and negative forces have value. Slowly it weakened the violent political bias of childhood, not by putting interests in its place, but by mental habits which had no bias at all. Rather by instinct than by guidance, the boy turned to writing, and his professors gave his English composition a hesitating approval; but he never convinced his teachers that his abilities, at their best, warranted placing him on the rank-list among the first third of his class. He held the same opinion himself.

The first door of escape that seemed to offer a hope led into Germany, and James Russell Lowell opened it. Lowell, on succeeding Longfellow as Professor of Belles-Lettres, had duly gone to Germany and brought back whatever he found to bring. The literary world then agreed that truth survived in Germany alone, and Carlyle, Matthew Arnold, Renan, Emerson, with scores of popular followers, taught the German faith. Goethe was raised to the rank of Shakespeare; Kant ranked as a law-giver above Plato. Adams was glad to accept Lowell's invitation to read German privately in his study. Lowell leaned towards Concord rather than Boston, and Adams approached Concord much as he would have entered a Gothic Cathedral, knowing the priests regarded him as only a worm. To the Concord Church all Adamses were minds of dust and emptiness; and Henry, at eighteen, had begun to feel uncertainty about so many matters more important than Adamses that he was ready to admit his unworthiness if only he might penetrate the shrine.

He never reached Concord. From Lowell he got no revolutionary thought, but he got good-humored encouragement to do what amused him, which consisted in passing two years in Europe after finishing the four years of Cambridge.

Unluckily for this particular boy, social advantages were his only capital in life. He made no acquaintance at college which proved to have the smallest use in after life. Strangers might gain something from the college if they were hard pressed for social connections; H. H. Richardson, who came from far away New Orleans, made valuable friendships there. Adams would have attached himself to Richardson in any case, as he attached himself later to John La Farge, Augustus St. Gaudens, Clarence King, John Hay—none of whom were at Harvard.

So Adams, well aware that he could not succeed as a scholar, betook himself to the single ambition the college left him. He took to the pen. He wrote. The College Magazine printed his work; the College Societies listened to his addresses. No one cared enough to criticise except himself. His work seemed thin, commonplace, feeble. At best it showed only a feeling for form; an instinct of exclusion.

The literary student's prize, almost taking the place of the regular prizes of scholarship, was election as Class Orator. To his own astonishment, Adams found himself elected over the head of the first scholar—a more capable and more popular rival. To him the election seemed a miracle. What he could never measure was the bewildering impersonality of these young men who deliberately chose as their representatives precisely those of their companions who seemed least to represent them. He saw in them the most formidable array of judges he could ever meet, like so many mirrors of himself, an infinite reflection of his own shortcomings.

What he said in his Class Oration of 1858 he soon forgot. He remembered an eminent uncle remarking that, as the work of so young a man, the oration was singularly wanting in enthusiasm; and another elderly gentleman noticing the orator's "perfect self-possession." Self-possession indeed! If Harvard College gave nothing else, it gave calm. Self-possession was the strongest part of Harvard College, which certainly taught men to stand alone. Whether he should ever have anything to say remained to be proved. As yet he knew nothing. Education had not begun.

## Chapter 2

A fourth child has the strength of his weakness. Being of no great value, he may throw himself away if he likes, and never be missed. Charles Francis Adams felt no love for Europe, which, as he and all the world agreed, unfitted Americans for America; yet when Henry presented to indulgent parents his request to begin at a German university the study of the Civil Law—although neither he nor they knew what the Civil Law was, or any reason for his studying it—they consented, and walked with him to the railway-station at Quincy to bid him good-bye.

He sailed in November, 1858, on the Persia, the pride of the Cunard Line. On the third day the world ran into a heavy storm. He learned then a lesson that stood by him better than any university teaching ever did—the meaning of a November gale on the mid-Atlantic. The first month of travel altogether became the rapidest school of education he had yet found. How many impressions could be crowded into one day without making any education at all became the *pons asinorum* of tourist mathematics.

Then Liverpool, and Chester, and the romance of red-sandstone architecture. At Eaton Hall the boys were awed as Thackeray or Dickens would have felt in the presence of a Duke. The very name of Grosvenor struck a note of grandeur. Aristocracy was real. So was the England of Dickens; Oliver Twist and Little Nell lurked in every churchyard shadow, not as shadow but alive. The journey up to London through the Black District was another lesson—the plunge into darkness lurid with flames; the sense of unknown horror in this weird gloom. He had no idea that Karl Marx was standing there waiting for him, and that the process of education would have to deal with Karl Marx much more than with the professors of Harvard. The boy ran away from it, as he ran away from everything he disliked.

London was still London. A certain style dignified its grime; heavy, clumsy, arrogant, purse-proud, but not cheap; insular but large; absolutely self-confident. The eighteenth century held its own. He crossed to Antwerp; the thirteenth-century cathedral towered above a sixteenth-century mass of tiled roofs; the taste of the town was thick, rich, ripe, like a sweet wine. He felt his middle ages and the sixteenth century alive.

Dropped into Berlin one morning without guide or direction, the young man in search of education floundered in a mere mess of misunderstandings. Within a day or two he was running about with the rest to beer-cellars and music-halls, smoking bad tobacco, drinking poor beer, and eating sauerkraut and sausages. His friends had him registered as a student of the university, selected his professors and courses, bought him the Institutes of Gaius, and led him to his first lecture. The first proved his last.

What Berlin's Gymnasium and university failed to teach, an accidental afternoon in a beer-hall did: amid stale tobacco and Hausfrauen knitting, Beethoven's symphonic line stole into Adams's unconscious and opened a sense he had not known he possessed, even as the German drill on memory taught him its hard limits.
